cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: ESSENTIALIA NEGOTII vs ACCIDENTALIA NEGOTII in a sale — what is the difference?
cards.back:
ESSENTIALIA = object and price, the core of the sale; ACCIDENTALIA = non-essential but possible extra terms, based on private autonomy.
• Examples of ACCIDENTALIA: special delivery mode, payment by instalments, modified duties.
• If side agreements are intended, consensus must cover all of them.
• Dissent on an auxiliary point prevents the whole contract from arising.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: Suspensive vs resolutive condition (CONDICIO) in a sale — how does each work?
cards.back:
Suspensive: the contract takes effect only once the condition is met. Resolutive: valid from consensus, dissolved when the condition occurs.
• CONDICIO = future, uncertain event; a certain future event is a time clause (DIES).
• Example 32: 'if my ship returns safely from Greece, it is sold to you' — suspensive.
• Example 33: cart sold for 10.000, a gift if the seller wins at gambling — resolutive.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: Resolutive condition fulfilled after delivery: EX TUNC vs EX NUNC effect — how does the seller get the thing back?
cards.back:
EX TUNC: no CAUSA ever existed, so the seller is still owner → REI VINDICATIO. EX NUNC: ownership transfer stands → CONDICTIO or contract action.
• Which effect applies depends on the wording of the agreement.
• EX NUNC: only the CAUSA for keeping the goods lapses.
• Suspensive condition: even after delivery, only fulfilment creates the CAUSA for ownership.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: LEX MANCIPIO DICTA — what is it and what is its legal basis?
cards.back:
An oral side agreement made at the MANCIPATIO; binding under Lex XII Tab VI.1: UTI LINGUA NUNCUPASSIT, ITA IUS ESTO.
• Gist: what is declared orally at the MANCIPATIO shall be law.
• Typical for a slave: duty to manumit, ban on manumission, duty to export.
• For a female slave: prohibition of prostitution.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: Example 34 (cf Paulus D 18.1.56, Case 142): slave mancipated on condition she is not prostituted; buyer prostitutes her and resells. Rights of the seller?
cards.back:
Murena may vindicate the slave even from the third party Capito: on breach, ownership reverted to him.
• Facts: Murena mancipates her to Thermus, who prostitutes her and sells her to Capito.
• LEGES MANCIPIO DICTAE act not only IN PERSONAM but IN REM.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: What are PACTA ADIECTA in an EMPTIO VENDITIO?
cards.back:
Side agreements added to the consensual sale; like the ESSENTIALIA NEGOTII they become binding parts of the contract.
• Enforceable with the sale actions.
• Main types: LEX COMMISSORIA, PACTUM DISPLICENTIAE, IN DIEM ADDICTIO.
• Further: PACTUM DE RETROEMENDO, PACTUM PROTIMISEOS.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: LEX COMMISSORIA — content, purpose and type of condition?
cards.back:
Clause making the sale invalid if the buyer has not paid the full price by a set date (cf Pomponius D 18.3.2, Case 133).
• Protects the seller; usually paired with payment by instalments.
• The sale is subject to the resolutive condition of non-payment.
• Example 35: Nisos may pay Omphale in three quarterly instalments, else the contract fails.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: Does a sale under a LEX COMMISSORIA dissolve IPSO IURE on the buyer's default?
cards.back:
No — default only gives the seller an option to withdraw, triggered by the objective fact of non-payment (cf Pomponius D 18.3.2, Case 133).
• Rationale: automatic lapse would let the buyer escape the sale simply by not paying.
• Tempting for him e.g. if the object perished by VIS MAIOR or he regrets the deal.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: Property link: why can the seller use REI VINDICATIO when a sale falls away under a LEX COMMISSORIA (Example 35)?
cards.back:
TRADITIO is causal: ownership passes only with a IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS. If the sale is dissolved, that CAUSA lapses too.
• REI VINDICATIO = the owner's action against any possessor.
• Nisos has no EXCEPTIO REI VENDITAE ET TRADITAE — there is no sale anymore.
• Contrast MANCIPATIO: abstract, needs no IUSTA CAUSA.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: LEX COMMISSORIA vs modern reservation of ownership?
cards.back:
Economic counterparts — but under reservation of ownership the seller keeps ownership until the price is fully paid.
• Technically: transfer of ownership under the suspensive condition of paying the price.
• LEX COMMISSORIA: the sale itself is resolutively conditional.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: PACTUM DISPLICENTIAE — what is it and how did the jurists construe it?
cards.back:
Sale on approval / on trial: if the buyer is dissatisfied, the goods count as not bought.
• Mostly seen as a sale under a resolutive condition: the contract arises at once.
• The buyer may withdraw within the trial period.
• Fulfilment depends on one party's will → CONDICIO POTESTATIVA.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: Trial before any sale (Example 36: Dionysos offers Hera a vase for 50) vs PACTUM DISPLICENTIAE?
cards.back:
Classical jurists treat a suspensive potestative condition not as a contract but as a binding offer by the seller.
• During the trial only the buyer decides.
• Acceptance within the period → unconditional sale (Hera says within the week she wants it).
• PACTUM DISPLICENTIAE: contract already concluded, resolutively conditional.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: IN DIEM ADDICTIO — what does it allow, and what counts as a 'better offer'?
cards.back:
The seller may withdraw if he gets a better offer within a set time (cf Ulpian D 18.2.2 pr, Case 135).
• Seller's advantage: a buyer is secured while he still looks for a better offer.
• Better = higher price or better payment terms (earlier date, more convenient place).
• Also a bidder's greater solvency (cf Ulpian (Pomponius) D 18.2.4.6, Case 137).

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: IN DIEM ADDICTIO as suspensive vs resolutive condition — effect on transfer of ownership?
cards.back:
Suspensive: no IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS until fulfilment, so no transfer of ownership. Resolutive: CAUSA arises at once, lapses on termination.
• Suspensive: sale effective only if no better offer comes in during the period.
• Resolutive: effective at once, cancellable on a better offer.
• Terminated resolutive sale → seller may vindicate from the buyer (cf Ulpian D 6.1.41 pr, Case 136).

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Auxiliary agreements
cards.front: PACTUM DE RETROEMENDO vs PACTUM PROTIMISEOS?
cards.back:
DE RETROEMENDO: seller's option to buy back at a pre-fixed price. PROTIMISEOS: buyer may resell only to the original seller.
• Exercising the option brings the pre-defined repurchase contract into effect (cf Proculus D 19.5.12, Case 141).
• PROTIMISEOS restricts the buyer's disposal (cf Hermogenian D 18.1.75, Case 140).

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Non-performance and expectation interest
cards.front: Object perishes before vs after conclusion of the sale — initial vs subsequent impossibility?
cards.back:
Before conclusion: initial impossibility — no contract (possibly reliance damages). After conclusion, before performance: subsequent impossibility — valid contract.
• Subsequent + seller at fault → damages for non-performance.
• Subsequent + event outside the seller's responsibility → question of assumption of risk.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Non-performance and expectation interest
cards.front: Culpable non-performance: what is the seller's duty before delivery, and what does he owe if he breaches it?
cards.back:
He may neither wilfully nor negligently prevent or impair delivery; otherwise the impossible delivery is replaced by its money equivalent.
• Until delivery he is still owner, but his freedom of disposal is limited by the duty to deliver.
• Damages = buyer's interest in having the object (Ulpian D 19.1.1 pr, Case 87).
• That interest is the expectation interest.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Non-performance and expectation interest
cards.front: What is expectation interest, and how is it determined?
cards.back:
A party's interest in proper performance by the other — the loss suffered when the other fails to perform properly ("positive interest").
• Difference method: actual assets vs hypothetical assets after proper performance.
• Seller: the agreed price; on default also interest on arrears.
• Buyer: measured by the object's market value.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Non-performance and expectation interest
cards.front: Agatha buys a vase worth 150 from Bubo for 100; Bubo culpably fails to deliver. What is her expectation interest?
cards.back:
50 if she has not yet paid (150 − 100); 150 if she has already paid the 100.
• Advantageous deal: value exceeds price → net gain in assets.
• Often market value = price → no interest beyond the price.
• Even if the value is below the price, the buyer can always reclaim the price.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Non-performance and expectation interest
cards.front: Example 38 (cf Paulus D 19.1.21.3, Case 91): wheat not delivered; buyer skips a cover purchase and two slaves starve. What can he claim?
cards.back:
Only 30 — the extra cost of the possible cover purchase (130 − 100); nothing for the starved slaves.
• Goods obtainable elsewhere → expectation interest = extra cost of the substitute transaction.
• Modern: Obliegenheit to minimise damages; only the unpreventable part is compensated.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Non-performance and expectation interest
cards.front: Example 39 (Lykaon, flute-playing slave, penalty of 100): why can expectation interest exceed the slave's value?
cards.back:
The reference point is the specific buyer's wealth: the slave lets Lykaon avoid the penalty → 180 if he has paid.
• 180 = 80 (value) + 100 (penalty avoided).
• Only if he cannot make a timely substitute purchase.
• Example 40: last volume of a nine-volume set — the set (1.200) exceeds the parts (100 each).

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Non-performance and expectation interest
cards.front: Example 41 (Ago wilfully withholds Stichus, whom Lysippe resold to Europa for 120 with a stipulated penalty of 50): what may Lysippe claim?
cards.back:
170 if she has already paid Ago 100: the value plus lost profit of 20 plus the penalty of 50.
• DAMNUM EMERGENS = loss of the object itself; LUCRUM CESSANS = lost (resale) profit.
• Lost profit belongs to non-performance damages.
• A mere chance of profit not yet materialised is not compensable.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Non-performance and expectation interest
cards.front: Case 86 (Labeo (Paulus) D 19.1.54 pr): the sold slave breaks his leg carrying out the seller's order before delivery. Is the seller liable?
cards.back:
Labeo: not if it was an order he usually gave, also to unsold slaves. Paulus: liable if a careful paterfamilias would not have given it.
• Labeo: subjective standard — DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS REBUS.
• Paulus: objective standard of a DILIGENS PATER FAMILIAS — was the task dangerous?
• The seller is always liable for DOLUS MALUS and CULPA.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: Example 42 (Ramses: table burnt by lightning, vase clumsily dropped, bowl stolen before collection) — which problem does each loss raise?
cards.back:
Table: VIS MAIOR → assumption of risk. Vase: seller's fault → non-performance damages. Bowl: lesser accident → is the seller liable for CUSTODIA?
• Questions: is the seller freed from delivering, and is the buyer freed from paying?
• Specific goods at fixed prices → the sale was perfected on 1 May.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: What is PERICULUM (risk) in sale, and which kinds of accident are distinguished?
cards.back:
The hazard of accidental loss, destruction or deterioration — accidental meaning neither party is at fault.
• VIS MAIOR = acts of God.
• CASUS MINOR = lesser accidents (relevant for CUSTODIA).

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: VIS MAIOR — Roman description and typical examples?
cards.back:
VIS CUI RESISTI NON POTEST — force that cannot be resisted; unforeseeable or unavoidable events.
• Natural death, shipwreck, fire.
• Attacks by pirates or armed robber gangs; flight of slaves.
• Harm despite utmost care also counts (Example 43: robbers take borrowed silver at knifepoint).

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: CUSTODIA — which standard of care does it denote, and how does it differ from the LEX AQUILIA standard?
cards.back:
Utmost diligence, esp. guarding: TALIS DILIGENTIA, QUALEM QUISQUE DILIGENTISSIMUS PATER FAMILIAS SUIS REBUS ADHIBET (cf Gaius D 13.6.18 pr, Case 23).
• Lesser accidents = harm that such utmost care could have prevented.
• LEX AQUILIA: care of a DILIGENS (not DILIGENTISSIMUS) PATER FAMILIAS suffices.
• Some contracts impose it, e.g. the borrower's CUSTODIA liability.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: Property link: CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS — what does it mean, and how does the Roman sale depart from it?
cards.back:
'The owner feels the accident': in general the owner bears the risk of accidental loss.
• The buyer becomes owner by TRADITIO from an authorised seller.
• So, strictly, risk would pass only on TRADITIO (as in modern law).
• Roman sale: risk passes earlier — on perfection (PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS).

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS — source and core rule?
cards.back:
From perfection the buyer bears the risk of VIS MAIOR: PERFECTA EMPTIONE PERICULUM AD EMPTOREM RESPICIET (Paulus D 18.6.8 pr, Case 79/1).
• Covers loss, destruction or deterioration between perfection and delivery.
• Twofold: non-performance risk and payment risk.
• Not necessarily linked to TRADITIO, unlike modern law.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: Non-performance risk vs payment risk under PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS?
cards.back:
Non-performance risk: getting neither goods nor damages despite a valid contract. Payment risk: having to pay without receiving performance.
• Primary performance = the goods; secondary performance = damages.
• Payment risk matters only for a party already bearing non-performance risk.
• After VIS MAIOR post-perfection the buyer bears both.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: Example 44: Probus buys a specific vase (worth 120) from Daphne for 100; an earthquake destroys it after perfection, before delivery. Result?
cards.back:
No vase and no damages (non-performance risk), yet Probus must still pay 100 (payment risk).
• Earthquake = VIS MAIOR; Daphne is not at fault.
• Mere deterioration: likewise full price for defective performance.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: Why did Roman law put the risk on the buyer, and what limited this rule?
cards.back:
Cash sales prevailed; where delivery was deferred, not taking delivery at once was seen as the buyer's advantage.
• Requires perfection: goods ascertained, no suspensive condition or time limit left.
• So many VIS MAIOR impairments fell outside the rule.
• Non-mandatory: the parties could agree another allocation.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: VIS MAIOR between conclusion (EMPTIO CONTRACTA) and perfection — who bears what?
cards.back:
Stock reduced but performance still possible → seller bears it (GENUS NON PERIT). Performance impossible → buyer gets nothing, but pays nothing.
• Before perfection the buyer bears the non-performance risk, not the payment risk.
• The seller need not supply substitutes.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Assumption of risk — VIS MAIOR, CUSTODIA, PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS
cards.front: Example 45 (Priamos sells Ismene 20 of 300 amphorae; an earthquake destroys 170 — or the whole cellar): result?
cards.back:
170 lost: sale unaffected — he must select 20 of the remaining 130 on 15 August. Whole cellar lost: no oil, no price.
• He cannot claim he meant the 20 from the destroyed part.
• Limited sale of unascertained goods from that stock.
• Not ascertained → not perfected → no PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Perfection and lesser accidents
cards.front: EMPTIO CONTRACTA vs EMPTIO PERFECTA?
cards.back:
CONTRACTA: binding on agreement on object and price. PERFECTA: price fixed, object specified, no suspensive condition or term pending.
• Perfect = ready for execution: QUID, QUALE, QUANTUM? (cf Paulus D 18.6.8 pr, Case 79/1).
• Perfection does not require that delivery be due.
• Perfection is the prerequisite of PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Perfection and lesser accidents
cards.front: Checklist: which circumstances prevent perfection of a sale?
cards.back:
Unascertained goods, a pending suspensive condition or term, undetermined quantity or price, and (presumably) defective goods.
• A resolutive condition does NOT prevent perfection.
• Unit-price sale: not perfected until the quantity is counted (cf Gaius D 18.1.35.5, Case 62).
• Defective goods: perfected once the defect is cured (cf Ulpian D 21.1.59 pr).

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Perfection and lesser accidents
cards.front: Example 46 (Lydus buys 100 amphorae from Turia's store: 1 Jan sale, 1 Feb chalk-marked, 1 Apr collected) — when does risk pass?
cards.back:
On 1 February: the amphorae are ascertained, so the sale is perfected (cf Gaius D 18.1.35.7, Case 80).
• 1 January: price certain (2.000), goods not yet ascertained.
• Ascertainment turns a duty to deliver unascertained goods into one for specific goods.
• Usually joint, so the buyer keeps passing of risk close to TRADITIO.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Perfection and lesser accidents
cards.front: Umbrella bought 'if it rains tomorrow' (Diana/Terentius) vs racehorse sold for Phaon's birthday (Example 48) — when perfected?
cards.back:
Umbrella: suspensive condition — perfected only if it rains. Racehorse: suspensive term — perfected on the birthday.
• While the condition is uncertain, there is no perfected sale.
• Example 49: all barrels at 100 each — unperfected until they are counted.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Perfection and lesser accidents
cards.front: OBLIGATIO ALTERNATIVA in sale — who chooses, and when is the sale perfected?
cards.back:
One of two (or more) individually specified things is owed; in doubt the seller chooses, but the choice may be given to the buyer.
• Unperfected while it is open which thing is to be delivered.
• Normally perfected when the choice is exercised.
• Also when all items but one become impossible through VIS MAIOR.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Perfection and lesser accidents
cards.front: Case 84 (Paulus D 18.1.34.6): 'Stichus or Pamphilus' sold; both die by VIS MAIOR, one after the other or simultaneously. Must the buyer pay?
cards.back:
Yes — in both variants the buyer bears the risk as to one slave and pays the price without receiving anything.
• Variant 1: first death shrinks the pool → survivor ascertained → sale perfected.
• Second death then falls on the buyer: non-performance and payment risk.
• Variant 2: Paulus generalises — buyer always bears the risk for one of the two.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Perfection and lesser accidents
cards.front: Example 50: Aristo buys 100 metretes from Iokaste's cellar; the whole cellar is destroyed before ascertainment. Does Paulus' alternative-obligation solution apply?
cards.back:
Prevailing opinion: no — PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS seems not to apply (cf Gaius D 18.1.35.7, Case 80).
• Conceivable analogy: whichever 100 had been picked would have perished.
• Counter: perfection is a separate prerequisite for the passing of risk.
• Else every impossibility would count as perfection — pointless.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Perfection and lesser accidents
cards.front: Lesser accident (e.g. theft) before delivery — what are the two views on the seller's CUSTODIA?
cards.back:
(a) Seller owes CUSTODIA like a borrower → liable for expectation interest. (b) Only DILIGENS PATER FAMILIAS care → released from performance.
• (a): Paulus D 18.6.3 (Case 79/2); Ulpian D 18.6.4.1 (Case 82) 1st sentence.
• On (a) only VIS MAIOR frees the seller.
• On (b) the buyer bears non-performance risk, but not payment risk.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Perfection and lesser accidents
cards.front: Example 51: Cato buys a thing worth 120 from Helena for 100; it is stolen before delivery. CUSTODIA liability vs risk for CUSTODIA — outcomes?
cards.back:
With CUSTODIA liability: Helena owes 120, Cato 100 → set-off leaves 20 for Cato. Without: Cato gets nothing and owes nothing.
• The models differ only when expectation interest exceeds the price.
• Worth 100, sold for 100 → same result: no performance on either side.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Delay (MORA)
cards.front: MORA DEBITORIS — definition, and is fault required?
cards.back:
The debtor does not offer the owed, still-possible performance on the due date in the agreed form.
• Consequences in principle only if culpably caused: SI PER EUM STAT.
• Delay ≠ non-performance or risk cases, where the obstacle is permanent.
• Roman sources use MORA for any culpable deviation, incl. non-performance.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Delay (MORA)
cards.front: Ulpian D 19.1.13.8: why must the buyer offer the price when he sues EX EMPTO?
cards.back:
Because the seller may hold back the sold thing like a pledge: VENDITOR ENIM QUASI PIGNUS RETINERE POTEST EAM REM QUAM VENDIDIT.
• OFFERRI PRETIUM AB EMPTORE DEBET, CUM EX EMPTO AGITUR.
• Illustrates the debtor's duty to offer performance when due.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Delay (MORA)
cards.front: Seller in MORA DEBITORIS — what are the consequences?
cards.back:
He becomes liable even for later accidental loss, owes damages for the delay, and in serious cases the buyer may withdraw.
• Accidental loss → expectation interest instead of delivery (cf Ulpian D 19.1.1 pr, Case 87).
• Late slave: his earnings since the due date plus the buyer's lost earnings (Neratius D 19.1.31.1, Case 88).
• Staying in the contract unreasonable → BONA FIDES probably allowed withdrawal.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Delay (MORA)
cards.front: Example 52: Vibia forgets to deliver a specific vase due on 1 March; lightning destroys it on 2 March. Who bears the loss?
cards.back:
Vibia: in delay since 1 March, she answers also for accidental loss and owes Cato his expectation interest.
• Risk had passed to Cato on perfection (PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS).
• The seller's culpable delay shifts it back to her.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Delay (MORA)
cards.front: Example 53 (cf Hermogenian D 18.6.20(19), Case 89): Pausanias pays late; Niobe misses a bargain earring deal for lack of cash. Her claim?
cards.back:
Only default interest — not the lost profit from the missed earring deal.
• A buyer paying late owes default interest; the seller has no further damages claim.
• Idea: she should have borrowed; the interest reimburses her borrowing cost.
• Rate: the customary local rate for borrowing money.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Delay (MORA)
cards.front: MORA CREDITORIS — definition, relation to MORA DEBITORIS, and the seller's liability during it?
cards.back:
The creditor fails to accept performance properly offered; it excludes MORA DEBITORIS (no proper offer, no default of acceptance).
• Creditor's fault probably not required.
• Buyer in default: seller liable only for DOLUS and CULPA LATA.
• VIS MAIOR, lesser accident, slight negligence → buyer pays and gets nothing.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Delay (MORA)
cards.front: Case 85/1 (Paulus D 18.6.13(12)): uncollected beds placed on a public road are smashed by the aedile. Who bears the risk?
cards.back:
The buyer, who had not collected them on time — Paulus reports this as the prevailing view.
• The buyer was in MORA CREDITORIS.
• Aediles also acted as traffic police; the beds obstructed traffic.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Delay (MORA)
cards.front: MORA CREDITORIS with money debts — how could the debtor free himself?
cards.back:
By depositing what is owed at certain public places, e.g. temples.
• Probably from Diocletian (late 3rd c.) on, deposit discharged the debt like performance.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Delay (MORA)
cards.front: Case 93 (Ulpian D 18.6.1.3): the wine buyer does not turn up for measuring by the agreed date. What may the seller do?
cards.back:
After notice he could even pour the wine away — better, though, to keep it and claim storage costs.
• Storage costs from late acceptance: ACTIO VENDITI.
• Lost rent for barrels he could have let out is recoverable.
• He may hire barrels from a third party and charge the buyer.

cards.topic: Ch. V — Sale II: Delay (MORA)
cards.front: Case 92 (Pomponius D 19.1.9): the buyer of stones fails to remove them from the seller's land as agreed. Remedy?
cards.back:
The seller can sue the buyer on the sale for removal.
• The contract may make taking delivery a duty, not just a right.
• Buyer in MORA CREDITORIS (entitled) and MORA DEBITORIS (obliged to remove).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty in general
cards.front: Warranty for defects of title vs defects as to quality — Examples 54 and 55?
cards.back:
Title: a third party's right defeats the buyer (Ex 54: owner Niketas wins REI VINDICATIO). Quality: the thing itself is defective (Ex 55: diseased cow).
• Both surface after delivery and payment.
• Obligations do not end with delivery: warranty claims arise later.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty in general
cards.front: Warranty — what is its typical feature regarding the seller's fault?
cards.back:
Liability regardless of fault: the seller answers for defects whether or not he caused or culpably concealed them.
• Seller's DOLUS matters: it makes liability stricter.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty in general
cards.front: A defect appears — at which moment did it arise, and which regime applies?
cards.back:
Present at delivery (not arising after perfection) → warranty; between perfection and delivery → risk or non-performance; after delivery → no claim.
• Accident after perfection → assumption of risk; seller's fault → non-performance.
• Root cause present at delivery suffices (cow already infected).
• Later grounds of eviction are not the seller's concern (Paulus D 21.2.11 pr).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty in general
cards.front: Labeo (Trebatius) in Ulpian D 19.1.13.22: who bears the costs of curing a sold slave before delivery, or of his funeral?
cards.back:
The buyer — the seller recovers these costs with his action EX VENDITO.
• Under PERICULUM EST EMPTORIS the buyer bears illness and death after perfection.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty in general
cards.front: Can warranty be excluded by agreement? (cf Pomponius D 19.1.6.9, Case 101)
cards.back:
Yes, warranty rules are dispositive — but never for DOLUS MALUS: excluding it violates BONA FIDES.
• Even after a total waiver the buyer can sue a seller who knowingly kept quiet.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Can one validly sell a thing one does not own? Exceptions? (Ulpian D 18.1.28, Case 95/2)
cards.back:
Yes: ownership or power of disposal generally has no bearing on the validity of the sale.
• Exception: buying one's own thing is legally impossible.
• Exception: no valid sale of a RES FURTIVA if both sides know it is stolen.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Property link: sale vs conveyance — which questions belong to obligations, which to property law?
cards.back:
Obligations: validity of the sale and the parties' duties. Property: whether TRADITIO was effective and the recipient became owner.
• Sale = obligation-creating transaction (claim to delivery).
• Conveyance (TRADITIO, MANCIPATIO) = transfer of ownership.
• So a non-owner's sale is valid, but his conveyance cannot make the buyer owner.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: The seller of another's thing does not even possess it and cannot deliver — consequence?
cards.back:
Subjective impossibility (inability) does not release him: he owes expectation damages (cf Ulpian D 19.1.1 pr, Case 87).
• Gaius D 18.1.35.4: seller of another's thing, losing it by theft without fault, stays liable.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Property link: why does the buyer of another's thing risk eviction — and what is eviction?
cards.back:
NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET: the buyer gets possession, not ownership, so the owner can sue him IN REM.
• Owner's action: REI VINDICATIO against any possessor.
• Eviction = a third party successfully enforces his right in rem against the buyer.
• Also by ACTIO PUBLICIANA, or a limited real right (VINDICATIO PIGNORIS).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: What must a Roman seller guarantee as to title — UTI FRUI HABERE LICERE?
cards.back:
Peaceable possession — use, fruits, possession; unlike modern Austrian law he need not make the buyer owner.
• Briefly also LICERE HABERE (cf Julian D 21.2.8, Case 100).
• Counter-concept: principle of procuring ownership (modern Austrian law).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Principle of eviction — content and rationale?
cards.back:
Warranty-of-title claims generally depend on eviction; the bare failure to get ownership gives no claim.
• While possession is peaceable, the seller's performance is not (yet) defective.
• Usucapion cures the defect: buyer gains original ownership.
• Contrast: principle of procuring ownership — claims whether or not evicted.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Property link: how does USUCAPIO make the principle of eviction practical?
cards.back:
The buyer from a non-owner possesses as usucapient; once the period has run he gains original ownership — the defect in title is cured.
• Periods: one year for movables, two years for land.
• Requirements: RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS.
• The former owner loses his right, so no eviction can follow.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: When exactly does eviction occur? (cf Pomponius D 21.2.16.1, Case 103)
cards.back:
When the buyer surrenders the thing under the CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA, or is condemned to pay its assessed value.
• Also: buyer lost possession, sues IN REM and loses against the possessor.
• Chain: evicted sub-buyer claims first; then first buyer vs first seller (Marcellus D 21.2.61, Case 105).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Property link: CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA and condemnation in the REI VINDICATIO — why do both count as eviction?
cards.back:
Unless the defendant restores the thing (CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA), he is condemned to pay its value (QUANTI EA RES ERIT).
• OMNIS CONDEMNATIO PECUNIARIA EST — the judge cannot order return itself.
• Either way the buyer loses the thing or pays for it.
• Both = successful enforcement of the third party's right in rem.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Claims upon eviction — which remedy for which kind of sale?
cards.back:
Mancipation sale → ACTIO AUCTORITATIS; stipulation given → action on the stipulation; plain EMPTIO VENDITIO → ACTIO EMPTI.
• ACTIO AUCTORITATIS: DUPLUM of the price.
• STIPULATIO DUPLAE: CONDICTIO for double the price.
• ACTIO EMPTI: expectation interest.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Property link: MANCIPATIO and AUCTORITAS — what is the seller's duty in a mancipation sale?
cards.back:
AUCTORITATEM PRAESTARE: to assist the buyer in the proceedings whenever a third party sues to enforce a right in rem.
• MANCIPATIO: formal IUS CIVILE act conveying quirite ownership of RES MANCIPI.
• Abstract but derivative — a non-owner cannot convey (NEMO PLUS IURIS).
• Eviction despite assistance → ACTIO AUCTORITATIS for the DUPLUM.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Example 56 (Appius → Silakes; Lyso vindicates): the buyer does not call in the seller and is evicted. Does his ACTIO AUCTORITATIS succeed?
cards.back:
Appius may raise the defences he could have raised against Lyso — here the EXCEPTIO REI VENDITAE ET TRADITAE.
• Seller not called in → keeps his defences (cf § 931 ABGB).
• Appius had got the RES MANCIPI from its owner by mere TRADITIO: bonitary owner.
• That exception is the bonitary owner's defence against the civil owner who sold and delivered.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: STIPULATIO DUPLAE — what does the seller promise, and how is it enforced?
cards.back:
REM EMPTAM ET TRADITAM NON EVICTAM ESSE — usually for double the price (DUPLUM).
• On eviction the buyer sues with a CONDICTIO for double the price.
• Another multiple may be agreed; none agreed → SIMPLUM (Javolenus D 21.2.60, Case 96).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: When was the seller bound to give a STIPULATIO DUPLAE, and what if he did not?
cards.back:
Seemingly for slaves bought at market, valuables and provincial land (Ulpian D 21.2.37.1, Case 99; Gaius D 21.2.6, Case 97).
• Refusal → buyer sues with the ACTIO EMPTI to make him give it.
• Eviction without stipulation → ACTIO EMPTI for what a stipulation would have yielded (Paul Sent 2.17.2).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: ACTIO EMPTI after eviction — what does the buyer recover? (Julian D 21.2.8, Case 100)
cards.back:
Expectation damages: the value of the thing plus every advantage lost through the eviction.
• Described as interest that the thing had been the seller's, or that the buyer becomes owner.
• Slave: also an inheritance he entered on the buyer's order.
• Female slave: also her child (PARTUS ANCILLAE).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Example 57 (Pomona → Omphale 100 → Quinta 120, both with STIPULATIO DUPLAE; owner Eros evicts Quinta): what can Quinta and Omphale claim?
cards.back:
Quinta: 240 from Omphale on the stipulation. Omphale: 200 on her stipulation — or 240 by ACTIO EMPTI, the better choice.
• Even with a STIPULATIO DUPLAE the buyer may sue on the sale (cf Javolenus D 21.2.60, Case 96).
• Worthwhile when expectation interest exceeds the stipulated sum.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Warranty of title WITHOUT eviction — which exceptions exist?
cards.back:
(a) Seller knew he could not dispose; (b) stipulated duty to procure ownership; (c) peaceable possession EX ALIA CAUSA.
• (a) ACTIO EMPTI for the interest in ownership (Africanus (Julian) D 19.1.30.1, Case 102).
• (b) action on the stipulation (Ulpian D 18.1.25.1, Case 95/1).
• (c) ACTIO EMPTI from BONA FIDES — but no action on a STIPULATIO DUPLAE.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: The seller knowingly sold and delivered another's goods — may the buyer sue before eviction? (Africanus (Julian) D 19.1.30.1, Case 102)
cards.back:
Yes: ACTIO EMPTI against the dishonest seller, without eviction, for his interest in having acquired ownership.
• Basis: BONA FIDES, which the seller violates by his dishonesty.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: Stipulated duty to procure ownership — what is a guarantee, and what can the buyer claim?
cards.back:
A guarantee = promise of compensation if a result (here: buyer becomes owner) is not achieved, regardless of fault.
• Buyer may sue on the stipulation, eviction or not (Ulpian D 18.1.25.1, Case 95/1).
• Scope per promise — typically a fixed sum, e.g. a multiple of the price.
• Only informal agreement → seemingly ACTIO EMPTI even before eviction.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Warranty of title — eviction
cards.front: The buyer of another's thing becomes the owner's heir, or buys it from the owner (Cases 106, 107). Claim against his seller?
cards.back:
Yes: ACTIO EMPTI from BONA FIDES — his possession is undisturbed EX ALIA CAUSA, by succession, not by the seller's performance.
• Heir = universal succession (Paulus D 21.2.9, Case 107); purchase = singular (Pomponius D 21.2.29 pr, Case 106).
• No action on a STIPULATIO DUPLAE: technically no eviction (Paulus D 21.2.9, Case 107).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: What is a defect as to quality?
cards.back:
A defect (physically) inherent in the thing sold that impairs its ordinary or expressly agreed use.
• Ordinary use: qualities normally expected of things of its kind — objective norm.
• Agreed use: promised qualities missing — oral assurances = DICTA ET PROMISSA.
• Decisive is the parties' agreement: ID QUOD ACTUM EST.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: Quality defects judged by the objective norm vs by agreement — which examples do the sources give?
cards.back:
Objective: rotten building timber (Case 116), leaking amphorae (Case 114); a sold claim must exist, not be collectable (Case 111).
• Agreed: vessel below assured capacity (Case 114); 'virgin' slave who is not (Case 121).
• 'Excellent cook' → truly excellent; 'cook' → average (Gaius D 21.1.18.1, Case 131).
• Clothes sold as second-hand: wear is no defect (cf Marcian D 18.1.45, Case 117).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: CAVEAT EMPTOR and sales talk — when is there no warranty?
cards.back:
Apparent defects give no claim — the buyer must examine (cf Florentinus D 18.1.43 pr, Case 118); mere praise binds nobody.
• 'Good-looking' slave: buyer checks himself; 'has learnt a trade': seller answers for it.
• Sales talk: no warranty where clearly not meant to bind (Ulpian (Pedius) D 21.1.19 pr, Case 132).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: Seller's duty of disclosure under BONA FIDES — what does Florentinus D 18.1.43.2 say?
cards.back:
DOLUM MALUM A SE ABESSE PRAESTARE VENDITOR DEBET — the seller must disclose defects and answer for being free of DOLUS MALUS.
• DOLUS covers speaking unclearly to mislead (OBSCURE LOQUITUR).
• And cunning concealment: QUI INSIDIOSE OBSCURE DISSIMULAT.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: Example 58 (cf Gaius D 18.1.35.8, Case 113): Leda sells her estate without telling Bruno that his mortal enemy owns the neighbouring estate. Result?
cards.back:
Bruno has warranty claims against Leda — she knew and did not disclose at conclusion.
• Basis: the seller's duty of disclosure under BONA FIDES.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: Who were the curule aediles, and why do they matter for warranty?
cards.back:
Roman magistrates supervising and judging the markets; as magistrates they held the IUS EDICENDI (power to issue general decrees).
• Their edicts on buying slaves and livestock at market shaped warranty law.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: Aediles' edict: what had a seller of slaves or animals to disclose?
cards.back:
For slaves: MORBUS and VITIA — FUGITIVUS, ERRO, and noxal liability (Ulpian D 21.1.1.1, Case 123/1).
• IUMENTA (draught/pack animals): MORBUS or VITIUM (Ulpian D 21.1.38 pr, Case 123/2).
• PECORA (herd animals) likewise (Ulpian D 21.1.38.5).
• Other animals were not covered by the edict.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: MORBUS and VITIUM in the edict — slight fever, missing tooth, missing tongue, runaway tendency, gambling?
cards.back:
MORBUS = any illness except minor ones: slight fever or small wound no; missing tooth no; missing tongue yes.
• Ulpian D 21.1.1.8 (Case 124/1); Paulus D 21.1.11 (Case 125); Ulpian (Ofilius) D 21.1.8 (Case 124/2).
• FUGITIVUS once he has shown an inclination to run away (Ulpian (Caelius) D 21.1.17.8, Case 127).
• Gambling, drinking, lying, quarrelsomeness: outside the edict (Ulpian D 21.1.4.2, Case 126).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: Which two functions does the edict's duty of disclosure serve?
cards.back:
It informs the buyer (he pays a correspondingly lower price — equivalence) and creates a guarantee that the thing is free of listed defects.
• Seller liable whether or not he knew of the defect.
• Basis: failure to inform the unaware buyer, or false assurances.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: ACTIO QUANTI MINORIS vs ACTIO REDHIBITORIA — aim and time limit?
cards.back:
QUANTI MINORIS: price reduction, within twelve months of the sale. REDHIBITORIA: rescission with mutual restitution, within six months.
• The buyer may choose.
• Reduction = what he would have paid less had he known of the defect.
• Both restore the equivalence the defect upset.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: ACTIO REDHIBITORIA — what does it achieve and what must be restored?
cards.back:
Buyer is put where he would be had he never contracted: contract dissolved EX TUNC, mutual restitution.
• Goods and price returned; buyer reimbursed costs (e.g. fees), surrenders benefits.
• Consequential loss may count: runaway slave steals → seller pays or surrenders him (NOXAE DEDITIO).
• Return of the goods is in principle a prerequisite.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — aediles' edict and remedies
cards.front: Case 128 (Ulpian D 21.1.31.11): the slave with an undisclosed defect dies before the buyer can return him. Can he still redhibit?
cards.back:
Yes. Death without the buyer's fault: redhibition without compensation (MORTUUS REDHIBETUR). By his fault: only if he compensates the lost value.
• Fault of the buyer, his servants or procurator → slave treated as still alive.
• Accidental death: the seller bears the risk.
• Fits especially if the slave died of the very illness grounding redhibition.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — ACTIO EMPTI and guarantees
cards.front: Quality defects outside the edict (not slaves or animals) — which action, and how was the edictal model used?
cards.back:
The ACTIO EMPTI: via BONA FIDES the aedilician rules became the norm also outside the aediles' jurisdiction.
• Applies to what counts as a defect and to the legal consequences.
• Price reduction (Cases 116, 115) and redhibition (Ulpian D 19.1.11.3, Case 121).
• Quality stipulation: action on it for ID QUOD INTEREST, normally not double.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — ACTIO EMPTI and guarantees
cards.front: Case 121 (Ulpian D 19.1.11.5): the seller knowingly lets the buyer believe a female slave is a virgin. Remedies?
cards.back:
No REDHIBITIO, but the ACTIO EMPTI to rescind, with restitution of the performances.
• Keeping her: presumably price reduction.
• Lack of virginity is no MORBUS or VITIUM under the edict.
• Alternatively: the slave was perhaps not bought at market.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — ACTIO EMPTI and guarantees
cards.front: Loss caused by a defect vs consequential loss — Examples 59 and 60 (Ago's timber)?
cards.back:
Defect loss: the thing itself is worth less (paid 1,000, worth 150 → 850). Consequential: harm to other assets (crushed desk, 4,000).
• Price reduction or restitution cover only the defect loss.
• Consequential loss only via ACTIO EMPTI if BONA FIDES was breached (fault-based).
• Modern codes separate them likewise (e.g. § 933a ABGB).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — ACTIO EMPTI and guarantees
cards.front: When does the ACTIO EMPTI give full damages including consequential loss?
cards.back:
When the seller breached BONA FIDES: knowingly concealed the defect, deceived by fraudulent assertions, or gave DICTA ET PROMISSA that prove false.
• Assurances: liable even without knowing of the defect (guarantee).
• Unaware seller, no assurance → only reduction or rescission.
• Cicero: Pythius staged fishermen to sell Canius his seaside villa.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — ACTIO EMPTI and guarantees
cards.front: Case 116 (Ulpian (Julian) D 19.1.13 pr): a sick animal infects the buyer's herd; defective timber makes a building collapse. Liability?
cards.back:
Seller unaware: only what the buyer would have paid less. Seller aware: all losses resulting from the purchase.
• Aware: value of the collapsed building; interest in having bought a healthy animal.
• The book prints 'the seller's interest' — presumably meant: the buyer's.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — ACTIO EMPTI and guarantees
cards.front: Case 117 (Marcian D 18.1.45): second-hand clothes knowingly sold as new to an unaware buyer. What does he get?
cards.back:
His interest — QUOD INTEREST (Trebatius, reported by Labeo; Pomponius and Julian agree).
• Julian: unaware seller liable for the value; aware seller also for the buyer's loss.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — ACTIO EMPTI and guarantees
cards.front: Case 115 (Ulpian (Julian) D 19.1.13.1): the slave sold is a FUGITIVUS, or a FUR. Seller's liability if he knew / did not know?
cards.back:
Knew: the buyer's interest in not having been deceived. Unaware: runaway → price reduction; thief → no liability.
• FUGITIVUS must be disclosed under the edict → defect even if seller unaware.
• FUR not in the edict → defect only if seller knew or assured otherwise.
• Sellers often stipulated that the slave was no FUR.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — ACTIO EMPTI and guarantees
cards.front: Case 114 (Pomponius D 19.1.6.4): vessels sold with assured capacity, with assured soundness, or with no assurance — and they leak. Liability?
cards.back:
Assurance → liable, incl. leaked wine. No assurance: one view requires DOLUS MALUS; Labeo (prevailing): seller answers for soundness anyway.
• Sabinus' parallel on rented barrels (cf Ulpian D 19.2.19.1, Case 154).
• The fault principle of the ACTIO EMPTI yields to (implied) guarantees.

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — ACTIO EMPTI and guarantees
cards.front: Case 122 (Paulus D 19.1.21.2): a table sold as thuja wood is not. Liability — and the alternative reading?
cards.back:
Seller liable for the buyer's interest in not having been deceived, whether or not he knew — presumed guarantee.
• As transmitted: valid sale, quality defect on delivery.
• Reading EMPTIONEM <NON> ESSE: error as to quality → no sale.
• Then QUOD INTEREST NON ESSE DECEPTUM = reliance interest (cf Modestinus D 18.1.62.1, Case 67).

cards.topic: Ch. VI — Sale III: Quality defects — ACTIO EMPTI and guarantees
cards.front: Decision tree: the buyer discovers a quality defect after delivery — which remedy?
cards.back:
Slave or animal with an edictal defect → REDHIBITORIA (6 months) or QUANTI MINORIS (12 months); otherwise ACTIO EMPTI to the same effect.
• Apparent defect or mere sales talk → no claim.
• Seller knew and concealed, or false DICTA ET PROMISSA → ACTIO EMPTI for full interest.
• Quality stipulation → action on it for ID QUOD INTEREST.
